title: Jews by choice
hookLine: converts, like Ruth, are fully Jewish; reminding them of their past is forbidden

cards: A dusty road out of Moab. Three widows walking. The oldest, Naomi, is going home to Bethlehem, and she tells her two daughters-in-law to go back to their own mothers.

Orpah kisses her and goes, and the text doesn't blame her. Ruth holds on, and tells her: "whither thou goest, I will go; and where thou lodgest, I will lodge; thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God."
Today is about people who say that sentence with their lives.

teach.b: Jewish tradition reads Ruth as a convert, someone not born Jewish who chose to join the people and its God. Hebrew calls such a person a ger tzedek, a righteous convert.

The word ger in the Torah means a stranger, someone who lives among you, and the Torah is firm about the stranger: "The stranger that sojourneth with you shall be unto you as the home-born among you, and thou shalt love him as thyself; for ye were strangers in the land of Egypt."
The rabbis read that verse, among others, about converts. And the Mishnah sets a rule about words that wound: to someone from a family of converts, you may not say, remember what your ancestors did.
You don't make them a guest in their own house. In Jewish law, once someone has converted, they are fully Jewish. Not almost.
Not Jewish with a footnote. When a convert asked the medieval sage Maimonides whether he could say in the prayers, our God and God of our fathers, Maimonides answered yes: Abraham is his father too.
And the book of Ruth ends with Ruth marrying Boaz; her great-grandson is David, the king. Israel's royal line runs through a woman from Moab who chose.
Today people convert within each of the Jewish movements, after study, usually before a rabbinic court, and often with immersion in a ritual bath.
The movements differ on the details and on whose conversions they accept, and those differences are real. But the rabbis' teaching is plain: a person who chose is not a lesser Jew.

how: Conversion to Judaism involves study with a rabbi and usually appearing before a rabbinic court, and often immersion in a mikveh; movements differ in their requirements, and Jewish law forbids reminding a convert of their past.

games.q: you're Ruth. your husband has died, and your mother-in-law Naomi tells you to go back to your own people. what do you do?
o: go home to Moab, like Orpah.
stay with Naomi, and take her people and her God as yours.
stay in Moab and send her alone.
games.why: Ruth holds on: "thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God." and her great-grandson becomes King David.

practice: Someone joined a group you belong to rather than being born into it: an in-law, a new neighbor, someone who came to your faith or your country. Notice whether, somewhere in you, they are still the new one.
Picture saying something that makes it plain they belong, without a word about where they came from.

wordCard.voice: Ger tzedek. A righteous convert, someone who chose to join the Jewish people, and who, like Ruth, is fully Jewish, with a past no one may throw at them. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: a righteous convert; ger first meant a stranger living among the people.

carryVoice: Your line: fully jewish. Ruth's road ended in a royal family. That's one thousand forty-six days.
